stem: Riya ties two identical stones to equal-length threads on her balcony hook. She pulls one aside by 5° and the other by 10° (both small angles) and releases them together. Which stone comes back to its starting point first?

options.A: The 10° stone, because it moves faster
options.B: The 5° stone, because its path is shorter
options.C: Both come back at the same time
options.D: It depends on which stone is slightly heavier

r1.text: The 10° one has more distance to go, so it needs more time.

r2.text: The 10° one goes farther but also moves faster, and these balance out, so the time is the same.

r3.text: The 10° one starts higher so it rushes down faster and gets back first.

stem: In the school lab, Neha's simple pendulum is 1.0 m long and swings with an amplitude of 4°. She restarts it with an amplitude of 8° (still a small angle). Take g = π² m/s². What is the period now?

r1.text: Double the swing means double the path, so the time doubles too.

r2.text: A wider swing gives more speed at the bottom, so it gets back sooner.

r3.text: The formula only has L and g, amplitude isn't in it, so the period doesn't change.

calc: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1.0/π²) = 2π/π = 2.0 s (same for 4° and 8°); SLIP C: 2π(L/g) without the root = 2/π ≈ 0.64 s

stem: Dadi's old pendulum wall clock in Pune is running down, so its pendulum's swing keeps getting smaller (always a small angle). What happens to the time taken for each swing?

options.B: It gets shorter, so the clock runs fast
options.C: It gets longer, so the clock runs slow
options.D: It depends on how heavy the brass bob is

r1.text: A smaller swing covers less distance but also moves slower, so each swing takes the same time.

r2.text: A smaller swing has less to travel, so it finishes quicker.

r3.text: A smaller swing moves slower, so it takes longer to finish.

verify_flags: Real clocks have a tiny amplitude-dependent (circular) error beyond small angles; ignored here as NCERT treats small-angle period as amplitude-independent.

stem: Ramesh, a mason, checks a wall with a 100 g plumb bob on a 0.25 m string; it swings gently (small angle). He swaps it for a 400 g bob on the same string. Take g = π² m/s². What is the new period?

r1.text: The heavier bob gets pulled down harder, so it swings back quicker.

r2.text: More mass means more pull but also more to move, so it cancels; only length and g matter.

r3.text: Four times the mass is harder to move, so it swings slower, like a heavier load on a spring.

verify_flags: Treats plumb bob as a point mass on a light string (simple pendulum).
